title: When Does Depth Help? Understanding Layerwise Inference in Tabular Foundation Models

paper.title: When Does Depth Help? Understanding Layerwise Inference in Tabular Foundation Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Transformer-based tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on small to medium-sized tabular prediction tasks while processing diverse inputs through a shared stack of layers. Recent layerwise analyses identify strong predictive performance in early TFM representations and substantial overlap in computation across layers. However, early predictive accessibility alone does not establish whether later layers are dispensable for every input, and aggregate accuracy can obscure which inputs benefit from additional computation. We study all 24 in-context-learning layers of TabPFN-3 across 272 classification datasets, combining representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions, while also examining related representation dynamics in four additional TFMs. We uncover a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory, with stronger late dimensional contraction associated with larger increases in class-prototype separation. A targeted analysis of early-stabilizing samples shows that substantial representational changes persist after predicted classes stabilize, while locally ambiguous queries obtain larger accuracy gains from shallow to late layers than well-separated queries. Repeating a single pretrained block or perturbing layer order reduces predictive performance on average, constraining simple post-hoc substitutions in the frozen model. These findings distinguish predictive accessibility, class stability, and the benefits of continuing computation, supporting an input-dependent assessment of depthwise redundancy in TFMs.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ; Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Garg et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Ma et al., 2025 ) use in-context learning to predict on new datasets from labeled support examples, without task-specific parameter updates. A single pretrained model processes tasks with different feature spaces and class structures through the same stack of in-context-learning layers. Understanding how much different inputs benefit from this depth is important for assessing computational redundancy and identifying opportunities to reduce inference cost while preserving prediction quality ( Elbayad et al., 2020 ; Fan et al., 2020 ) . Recent layerwise analyses identify strong predictive performance in early TFM representations and substantial overlap in computation across layers ( Balef et al., 2026 ) . TabSwift ( Liu and Ye, 2026 ) further demonstrates per-query early exiting and observes that deeper exits concentrate in ambiguous regions of representation space. These findings motivate examining what subsequent computation still contributes. Early predictive accessibility does not establish that later layers are dispensable for every input, and aggregate accuracy can obscure which inputs benefit from them. Our layerwise evaluation of TabPFN-3 makes this distinction concrete. When queries are grouped by local class separation within each dataset, locally ambiguous groups show larger absolute accuracy gains from L9 to L23 on average than well-separated groups (Figure 1 (a)). Meanwhile, a targeted analysis of early-stabilizing samples shows that their representations continue to change substantially after their predicted classes stabilize, including pronounced late dimensional contraction (Figure 1 (b)). These observations highlight the need to distinguish predictive accessibility, class stability, and the accuracy gains from additional computation. They motivate our central question: When does later computation remain predictively useful, and how does its value vary across inputs? Figure 1: Predictive accessibility, class stability, and the value of depth are distinct. (a) L9/L13/L23 accuracy vs. local class separation: ambiguous queries gain more from depth. (b) Effective dimensionality per layer for early-stabilizing queries: representations keep changing after the class stabilises, then contract sharply. We study all 24 ICL layers of TabPFN-3 using 272 classification datasets from OpenML-CC18 ( Bischl et al., 2019 ) and TALENT ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . We complement its native attention-based retrieval decoder ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) with layer-matched classifiers and decoder-independent probes, combining representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions. We also examine related representation dynamics in four additional TFMs ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Grinsztajn et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) . We find that TabPFN-3 representations follow a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory: early expansion is followed by a relatively stable middle regime and substantial reorganization near the output. Class-relevant information is readable at shallow depth, while class-prototype separation strengthens mainly at later layers. Across datasets, stronger late dimensional contraction is associated with greater increases in prototype separation. These findings distinguish the early availability of predictive information from the subsequent evolution of representation geometry. At the task level, datasets with later prediction stabilization tend to incur larger accuracy losses under truncation. The overall depthwise accuracy gain also cannot be attributed entirely to mismatch with the final decoder: across 72 OpenML-CC18 tasks, accuracy increases from 82.2% at L2 to 85.6% at L23 when each layer is evaluated using its own fitted readout. Additional computation therefore retains predictive value beyond what is accessible through shallow representations under these readouts. Finally, interventions show that the frozen model is sensitive to changes in its learned layer composition. Replacing distinct blocks with repeated applications of a single pretrained block, or perturbing their execution order, alters representation dynamics and reduces predictive performance on average. These results constrain simple post-hoc substitutions within the pretrained computation. Our findings support evaluating depthwise redundancy through input-dependent predictive gains alongside the accompanying representation dynamics, and motivate future work on adaptive-depth TFM inference.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Tabular Foundation Models. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) build on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) to perform in-context learning without task-specific parameter updates ( Müller et al., 2022 ) . TabPFN-v1 performs ICL over row-level representations, whereas TabPFN-v2 moves to cell-level representations with alternating row- and feature-wise attention; TabPFN-2.5 largely retains this design while increasing depth and scaling to larger tables ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ; Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Grinsztajn et al., 2025 ) . In parallel, TabICL introduces a compression-then-ICL architecture that first constructs fixed-dimensional row representations, with TabICLv2 further extending this design through repeated feature grouping and target-aware representations ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) . LimiX expands structured-data foundation modeling through joint conditional prediction and retrieval-based ensemble inference ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , while TabPFN-3 combines feature grouping and row compression in a three-stage architecture ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . Despite this architectural progress, mechanistic understanding of TFM inference remains limited. Existing studies have examined spectral adaptivity ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , learned feature-space structure ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , intermediate-representation decodability ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ) , and layerwise predictive refinement and redundancy ( Balef et al., 2026 ) . Our work complements these studies by jointly examining representation geometry, sample-level prediction dynamics, and the functional role of depth. Layerwise Analysis of Transformer Representations. Layerwise analysis has been widely used to trace how information and computation evolve across Transformer depth. Probing and tuned readouts characterize when task-relevant information becomes accessible ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ; Hewitt and Manning, 2019 ; Tenney et al., 2019 ; Rogers et al., 2020 ; Belinkov, 2022 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ) , while representation-similarity and geometric analyses characterize how internal representations change across layers ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ; Ansuini et al., 2019 ; Skean et al., 2025 ) . Complementary intervention-based studies test whether individual layers or their ordering are functionally consequential ( Lad et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . Most directly, Balef et al. (2026) identify early predictive accessibility, iterative refinement, and substantial depthwise redundancy in TFMs. We extend this layerwise perspective beyond predictive readability to characterize how geometry and individual prediction trajectories evolve, and whether later transformations retain functional value. Views of Computation Across Depth. Depth has been interpreted as both iterative refinement and structured representation transformation. Residual networks can implement successive refinements of existing representations ( Jastrzebski et al., 2018 ) , whereas geometric studies report nontrivial depthwise changes in dimensionality and information structure ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ; Skean et al., 2025 ) . Related work on shared transformations and adaptive-depth inference further asks whether computation can be repeated, truncated, or selectively allocated across inputs ( Dehghani et al., 2019 ; Lan et al., 2020 ; Elbayad et al., 2020 ; Xin et al., 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ) . These perspectives leave open whether TFM depth primarily reflects repetitive refinement or an ordered sequence of distinct, selectively useful transformations.

sections.heading: 3.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Models. We use TabPFN-3 as the primary model for layerwise analysis ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . To assess cross-model generality, we additionally evaluate TabPFN-v2, TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and TabICLv2 ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Grinsztajn et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) . Architectural details are provided in Appendix A.1 , with cross-model results reported in Appendix C . Datasets and Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate binary and multiclass classification on 72 tasks from OpenML-CC18 ( Bischl et al., 2019 ) and 200 tasks from TALENT ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . We restrict the study to classification to maintain a common output space for analyzing layerwise prediction dynamics and representation geometry. All models use their standard preprocessing and inference pipelines. The layerwise representation-extraction protocol is detailed in Appendix A.2 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Layerwise Analysis Framework
sections.text: Analysis framework. We analyze layerwise inference from three complementary perspectives: representation geometry, sample-dependent prediction dynamics, and the functional role of depth, building on prior layerwise probing, readout, and TFM analyses ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ; Kornblith et al., 2019 ; Balef et al., 2026 ) . For query i i , we denote its hidden representation after layer ℓ \ell by h i ( ℓ ) h_{i}^{(\ell)} and track its representation and prediction across depth. The representation-extraction protocol is detailed in Appendix A.2 . Predictive readout. TabPFN-3 differs from earlier TabPFN variants in replacing the fixed-width classification head with an attention-based retrieval decoder ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . The decoder predicts directly from the relationship between query and support representations: support representations serve as keys, their one-hot labels as values, and query representations as queries. Because all 24 ICL layers preserve the same 512-dimensional hidden size and the decoder uses layer-independent projections, we can apply the same pretrained model-native decoder at every depth to obtain a consistent predictive readout across layers. To control for possible mismatch between this decoder and intermediate representations, we complement the native readout with layer-matched readouts. Full decoder definitions and validation results are provided in Appendix E.1 . Representation and functional analyses. We characterize representation geometry using effective dimensionality ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ) , PCA displacement, linear CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) , and cosine similarity, capturing complementary aspects of dimensionality, movement, global structural similarity, and sample-wise directional alignment. We trace sample-level prediction trajectories and apply structural interventions to test when additional depth becomes functionally consequential ( Lad et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Balef et al., 2026 ) . Metric definitions are provided in Appendix B , with supplementary prediction-dynamics and functional analyses in Appendices G and H , respectively.

sections.heading: 4.1 Representational Expansion Precedes Late Compression
sections.text: We first examine how representation geometry evolves across depth. We measure this evolution using PCA-based effective dimensionality (ED) ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ) . For the centered query representation matrix H ~ ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ n × d \widetilde{H}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with singular values σ 1 ≥ σ 2 ≥ ⋯ \sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\cdots , we define ED ⁡ ( H ( ℓ ) ) = min ⁡ { k : ∑ i = 1 k σ i 2 ∑ i σ i 2 ≥ 0.9 } . \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle\mathrm{ED}(H^{(\ell)})=\min\left\{k:\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}}\geq 0.9\right\}$}. ED measures the number of principal directions required to explain most of the representation variance. Full details are provided in Appendix B.2 . Figure 2: Representational expansion followed by late compression. Thin curves denote individual datasets and the thick curve denotes the dataset-level mean. Figure 2 reveals a pronounced non-monotonic trajectory. Effective dimensionality rises sharply at shallow depth, remains broadly elevated through the middle layers, and contracts near the output, with a brief local rebound preceding the final decline. We summarize these stages as expansion , plateau , and compression ; L9 and L17 serve only as descriptive anchors for subsequent analyses. This pattern reveals a characteristic geometric trajectory: early layers broaden the effective representational space, whereas substantial contraction emerges only near the output. We refer to this trajectory as Expansion–Compression . The pattern persists across retained-variance thresholds, normalization and covariance controls, and nearby regime boundaries. Random-weight initialization produces a qualitatively different depthwise profile (Appendix E.3 ; Appendix D.1 ). This late contraction occurs alongside continued representational change. We therefore next examine how strongly representations are reorganized within and across these regimes.

sections.heading: 4.2 Late Compression Involves Concentrated Reorganization
sections.text: Figure 3: Representation transformation dynamics across depth. (a) Mean pairwise layer similarity, with linear CKA above the diagonal and cosine similarity below. (b) Adjacent-layer displacement measured in a shared PCA basis. (c) Dataset-level displacement across the expansion, plateau, and compression regimes. The ED trajectory characterizes how broadly representation variance is distributed across depth. To quantify the strength of transformation within each regime, we complement ED with pairwise layer similarity, measured by linear CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) and cosine similarity, together with adjacent-layer displacement in a shared PCA space. Metric details are provided in Appendix B.3 . Figure 3 (a) reveals distinct depthwise transformation dynamics. During expansion, representations progressively depart from earlier layers. The plateau forms a pronounced high-similarity block across both nearby and distant layers, indicating relative mid-depth stabilization. Near the output, this block breaks down as the final layers increasingly diverge from the plateau representations. Representation displacement exhibits the same structure (Figure 3 (b)). Layer-to-layer movement remains substantial during expansion, reaches its minimum through the plateau, and rises sharply again at late depth.The final layer transitions exhibit the largest concentration of PCA displacement, indicating intensified representational reorganization near the output. This concentration is consistent across datasets, with displacement lowest during the plateau and highest in the compression regime (Figure 3 (c)). Late compression therefore coincides with a concentrated phase of geometric reorganization near the output. Representation transformation intensifies again after the mid-depth plateau, showing that substantial internal reorganization persists into the final layers.

sections.heading: 4.3 Early Predictive Accessibility Precedes Candidate Resolution

For each support class c c , we construct a layer-specific prototype μ c ( ℓ ) \mu_{c}^{(\ell)} and compute its cosine similarity with query i i , s i , c ( ℓ ) = cos ⁡ ( h i ( ℓ ) , μ c ( ℓ ) ) . s_{i,c}^{(\ell)}=\cos(h_{i}^{(\ell)},\mu_{c}^{(\ell)}). We quantify candidate competition by the margin between the two most similar class prototypes, Δ i ( ℓ ) = s i , ( 1 ) ( ℓ ) − s i , ( 2 ) ( ℓ ) , \Delta_{i}^{(\ell)}=s_{i,(1)}^{(\ell)}-s_{i,(2)}^{(\ell)}, and use the rank of the correct-class prototype to measure alignment with the target class. The analysis covers all 105 multiclass datasets from OpenML-CC18 and TALENT. Full diagnostic details are provided in Appendix F . Figure 4: Candidate separation strengthens at late depth. (a) Prototype margins remain small through the early and middle layers and widen most strongly near the output. (b) Correct-class alignment emerges earlier on easier tasks, whereas harder tasks retain candidate ambiguity deeper into the network. (c) Stronger late effective-dimensionality contraction is associated with larger increases in prototype margin. Figure 4 (a) shows that prototype margins remain small through the early and middle layers and widen most strongly near the output. Figure 4 (b) reveals a corresponding progression in correct-class alignment: easier tasks establish favorable alignment earlier, whereas harder tasks retain candidate ambiguity deeper into the network. Class-relevant information is already accessible well before strong candidate separation emerges. The attn@V probe exhibits strong linear class decodability by L2, whereas prototype margins widen primarily at later depth (Appendix F.3 ). Predictive accessibility therefore precedes strong geometric resolution among competing class candidates. We next relate late candidate resolution to the compression identified in Section 4.1 . For each dataset d d , we define relative late compression as C d = ED d ( 20 ) − ED d ( 23 ) ED d ( 20 ) , \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle C_{d}=\frac{\mathrm{ED}_{d}^{(20)}-\mathrm{ED}_{d}^{(23)}}{\mathrm{ED}_{d}^{(20)}}$}, and the corresponding increase in candidate separation as R d = Δ d ( 23 ) − Δ d ( 20 ) . R_{d}=\Delta_{d}^{(23)}-\Delta_{d}^{(20)}. Figure 4 (c) shows that datasets with stronger late compression exhibit larger increases in prototype margin. The same association persists across alternative specifications (Appendix F.4 ). Late dimensional contraction and candidate resolution therefore covary systematically across datasets. These results separate predictive accessibility from geometric resolution. Class-relevant information becomes readable at shallow depth while competing candidates remain weakly separated. Near the output, concentrated reorganization and compression coincide with stronger candidate separation and target-aligned geometry. Predictive accessibility therefore precedes geometric resolution.

sections.heading: 5.1 Prediction Commitment Is Sample-Dependent
sections.text: Section 4.3 shows that predictive accessibility can precede geometric resolution. We next turn to the sample level and ask when the predicted class itself becomes stable. For sample i i , we denote its layerwise prediction trajectory as p i = ( y ^ i ( 0 ) , … , y ^ i ( 23 ) ) p_{i}=(\hat{y}_{i}^{(0)},\ldots,\hat{y}_{i}^{(23)}) and define the stabilization depth as the earliest layer after which the predicted class remains identical to the final-layer prediction: s i = min { ℓ : y ^ i ( k ) = y ^ i ( 23 ) , ∀ k ≥ ℓ } s_{i}=\min\{\ell:\hat{y}_{i}^{(k)}=\hat{y}_{i}^{(23)},\,\forall k\geq\ell\} . We use predictive commitment to denote this stabilization of class identity. The resulting stabilization depth s i s_{i} is a retrospective trajectory-level quantity. Confidence and representation geometry may continue to evolve after commitment. Figure 5: Sample-level predictive commitment across depth. (a) Cumulative fraction of samples stabilized to the final prediction across layers, shown per dataset and in aggregate. (b) Five recurring prediction-transition patterns and their pooled prevalence. (c) Pattern composition across tertiles of chance-normalized task difficulty; statistical analyses use difficulty as a continuous variable. Figure 5 (a) reveals substantial heterogeneity in predictive commitment. Many predictions stabilize at shallow depth, while others continue to change through intermediate or late layers, with pronounced variation across datasets. Predictions therefore commit at markedly different depths. Stabilization depth captures when a prediction becomes stable, while the preceding trajectory reveals how its class identity evolves before commitment. We characterize this trajectory using prediction identities at L9, L13, and L23 together with the total number of class transitions across all 24 layers, n chg , i = ∑ ℓ = 1 23 𝕀 [ y ^ i ( ℓ ) ≠ y ^ i ( ℓ − 1 ) ] n_{\mathrm{chg},i}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{23}\mathbb{I}\bigl[\hat{y}_{i}^{(\ell)}\neq\hat{y}_{i}^{(\ell-1)}\bigr] . Pattern assignment uses only the prediction trajectory and does not depend on ground-truth correctness. Full assignment rules are provided in Appendix G.1 , with sensitivity to nearby representative-layer choices reported in Appendix G.3 . Figure 5 (b) summarizes five recurring trajectory patterns. Early-Stable (ES) predictions reach the final predicted class early and remain there; Transient-Switch (TS) predictions temporarily depart from it before returning; Intermediate-Switch (IS) and Late-Switch (LS) predictions reach the final class at intermediate and late depth, respectively; and Multi-Switch (MS) predictions undergo repeated class changes. ES is dominant at 72.2%, followed by TS (15.8%), LS (5.8%), IS (5.3%), and MS (1.0%). Although early commitment is predominant, more than one quarter of samples exhibit non-early prediction dynamics. Similar pattern distributions are observed under dataset-level aggregation and nearby representative-layer choices (Appendices G.2 – G.3 ). Representation dynamics continue beyond early predictive commitment. Early-Stable samples have stabilized by L9, while their representations still exhibit the characteristic Expansion–Compression trajectory, including pronounced late reorganization (Appendix G.5 ). Predictive commitment can therefore precede substantial later representational transformation. More broadly, all samples traverse the same sequence of layers, while their predictions commit at substantially different depths.

sections.heading: 5.2 Commitment Depth Tracks Task Difficulty and Local Ambiguity
sections.text: Commitment depth varies systematically with task difficulty and local ambiguity. At the task level, we define model-relative, chance-normalized difficulty as D d = 1 − a d − 1 / C d 1 − 1 / C d , \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle D_{d}=1-\frac{a_{d}-1/C_{d}}{1-1/C_{d}}$}, where a d a_{d} is final-layer accuracy and C d C_{d} is the number of classes. Harder tasks stabilize later on average, with a consistent association across alternative definitions of difficulty (Appendix G.4 ). Figure 6: Local class separation across prediction-transition patterns. Separation decreases from ES to MS, indicating local ambiguity for more dynamic trajectories. Correspondingly, Figure 5 (c) shows a systematic shift from ES toward non-ES trajectories as task difficulty increases. At the sample level, we quantify local ambiguity using class separation in the input space: r i = d ⁡ ( x i , NN diff ) d ⁡ ( x i , NN same ) , \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle r_{i}=\frac{d\!\left(x_{i},\mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{diff}}\right)}{d\!\left(x_{i},\mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{same}}\right)}$}, where NN same \mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{same}} and NN diff \mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{diff}} denote the nearest same- and different-class neighbors, respectively. Smaller r i r_{i} indicates greater local ambiguity. Median separation decreases from 1.52 1.52 for ES to 0.81 0.81 for MS (Figure 6 ). Dataset-aware comparisons further show higher separation for ES than for every non-ES pattern in approximately 95% of shared datasets (Appendix G.6 ). For cross-dataset analyses, we convert r i r_{i} to a within-dataset local-separation percentile to place datasets with different raw distance scales on a common reference. Lower percentiles correspond to more ambiguous samples, whereas higher percentiles indicate more clearly separated local neighborhoods. Commitment depth therefore varies systematically across both tasks and samples. Harder tasks commit later on average, while locally ambiguous samples exhibit more dynamic prediction trajectories. Thus, inputs traversing the same network can differ substantially in how much depth is required before their predictions stabilize.

sections.heading: 6.1 Additional Depth Has Selective Utility
sections.text: We next examine whether the heterogeneous commitment identified above is reflected in the functional value of additional computation at both the sample and task levels. Lower local-separation percentiles indicate greater ambiguity, whereas higher percentiles correspond to more clearly separated samples. Figure 7: Depth has selective utility across samples and tasks. (a) Accuracy at L9, L13, and L23 across within-dataset local-separation percentiles; locally ambiguous samples show larger gains with depth. (b) Retention of L9-correct predictions and rescue of L9 errors across local-separation percentiles; both increase with separation. (c) Mean stabilization depth is positively associated with L13 truncation loss. (d) Accuracy increases with depth under layer-matched readouts. At the sample level, Figure 7 (a) shows that depthwise benefit depends strongly on local ambiguity. Accuracy is already high at L9 for well-separated samples and changes only modestly toward L23, whereas the gap between shallow and final depth grows as local separation decreases. Locally ambiguous inputs therefore obtain larger aggregate gains from additional computation. To distinguish aggregate depthwise gains from the fate of individual shallow predictions, we separately measure retention of shallow successes and rescue of shallow errors: Retain = P ⁡ ( y ^ ( 23 ) = y ∣ y ^ ( 9 ) = y ) , Rescue = P ⁡ ( y ^ ( 23 ) = y ∣ y ^ ( 9 ) ≠ y ) . \mathrm{Retain}=P(\hat{y}^{(23)}=y\mid\hat{y}^{(9)}=y),\qquad\mathrm{Rescue}=P(\hat{y}^{(23)}=y\mid\hat{y}^{(9)}\neq y). Figure 7 (b) shows that both retention and rescue increase with local separation. Thus, ambiguous groups show larger aggregate gains overall, even though errors already present at L9 are less frequently rescued. The same trends hold with L8 or L10 as the shallow reference (Appendix H.2 ). The same selectivity appears at the task level. We define the loss from truncating inference at layer ℓ \ell as Δ ​ Acc d ( ℓ ) = Acc d ( 23 ) − Acc d ( ℓ ) . \Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{(\ell)}_{d}=\mathrm{Acc}^{(23)}_{d}-\mathrm{Acc}^{(\ell)}_{d}. Using L13 as the representative truncation point, Figure 7 (c) shows that datasets with later mean stabilization depth incur greater accuracy loss. The association remains positive for later truncation points and with balanced accuracy (Appendix H.1 ). Later-committing tasks are therefore more sensitive to truncation. The depthwise advantage also persists under depth-specific readouts. With independently trained layer-matched readouts, Figure 7 (d) shows that accuracy increases from 82.2 % 82.2\% at L2 to 85.6 % 85.6\% at L23. Greater depth therefore remains predictively beneficial when each layer is evaluated through its own matched readout. The functional value of depth is therefore selective: locally ambiguous samples obtain larger aggregate gains from additional computation, while later-committing tasks are more sensitive to truncation. Well-separated inputs, by contrast, gain comparatively little from the remaining layers.

sections.heading: 6.2 Later Computation Is Ordered Rather Than Repetitive
sections.text: We next characterize the structure of this later computation through interventions on the ICL stack, comparing repeated shared transformations with the sequence of distinct learned blocks. Figure 8: Shared-weight repetition produces a distinct depthwise trajectory. (a) Shared-weight repetition weakens compression and class-discriminative growth. (b) The repeated-block trajectory remains distinct at matched computational depth. (c) The full model retains a predictive advantage under perturbation. Replacing the sequence of distinct ICL blocks with repeated applications of a shared block substantially weakens both late compression and class-discriminative growth (Figure 8 (a)). The effective-dimensional compression ratio decreases from 2.85 × 2.85\times to 1.05 × 1.05\times , while the FDR gain decreases from 2.53 2.53 to 0.84 0.84 . The repeated-block trajectory remains qualitatively distinct even after 24 applications (Figure 8 (b)), with the same pattern observed for representative blocks selected from different stages (Appendix H.3 ). These representational differences are accompanied by predictive differences. Figure 8 (c) shows a positive average advantage for the original model under clean evaluation, label noise, feature perturbation, and reduced sample availability. Under 20 % 20\% label noise, this advantage holds on every evaluated task (Appendix H.4 ). The learned sequence of distinct blocks therefore yields both the characteristic representation trajectory and stronger predictive behavior than repeated generic computation. Figure 9: Layer order is functionally consequential. (a) Shuffling or reversing the learned sequence disrupts the depthwise representation dynamics. (b) Reordering reduces predictive performance on average. A complementary intervention preserves the learned blocks while changing only their execution order. Shuffling or reversing the learned sequence largely removes the characteristic late compression in the representation trajectory (Figure 9 (a)), while also reducing predictive performance on most evaluated tasks (Figure 9 (b)). Because the learned transformations are preserved, this intervention isolates execution order as a functional component of depth. Later computation is therefore structured as an ordered sequence of distinct learned operations. Its representational and predictive effects depend on both transformation identity and execution order. This computation path is shared across inputs, while their resolution requirements vary substantially.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Interpretation. Our study clarifies when later computation remains predictively useful and how its value varies across inputs. Class-relevant information becomes accessible at shallow depth, while representation geometry continues to evolve through an Expansion–Compression trajectory, with predictive accessibility preceding geometric resolution. At the sample level, predictions commit at substantially different depths, varying systematically with task difficulty and local ambiguity. This heterogeneity is reflected in the functional value of depth: locally ambiguous samples obtain larger aggregate gains from additional computation, later-committing tasks are more sensitive to truncation, and depthwise predictive gains remain under layer-matched readouts. Structural interventions further show that later computation depends on an ordered sequence of distinct learned transformations rather than generic repetition. These findings show that TFMs follow a shared computation path whose functional value varies substantially across inputs, motivating an input-dependent view of depthwise redundancy. Limitations and Future Work. Our analysis focuses primarily on TabPFN-3 and classification, although complementary experiments reveal related representation dynamics in several additional TFMs. The strength and temporal organization of Expansion–Compression may vary across architectures and model scales. A practical early-exit mechanism will require reliable online signals that estimate whether additional computation is likely to alter or improve a prediction, rather than relying on the retrospective stabilization depth used in our analysis. Future work could investigate inference-time signals derived from prediction confidence, trajectory consistency, or representation geometry, and determine how reliably they identify inputs that benefit from continued computation. Extending these analyses to broader TFM architectures and regression settings is another important direction, particularly because regression will require suitable continuous notions of predictive commitment rather than discrete class-identity stabilization.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: We have made every effort to ensure that the results presented in this paper are reproducible. The experimental setup, including the evaluated models, datasets, layerwise evaluation protocols, representation metrics, prediction analyses, and structural interventions, is described in detail in the main paper and appendices. We additionally provide the definitions of all major evaluation metrics, dataset-level aggregation procedures, statistical analyses, and robustness checks used throughout the study. The datasets used in our experiments are drawn from publicly available benchmark collections, including OpenML-CC18 and TALENT, enabling consistent and reproducible evaluation. Detailed descriptions of model architectures and layerwise representation extraction are provided in Appendix A, while Appendix B specifies the representation metrics and analytical procedures. Additional analyses of candidate geometry, prediction dynamics, truncation, matched readouts, shared-weight controls, data perturbations, and layer-order interventions are documented in the subsequent appendices. We believe these details provide sufficient information to facilitate replication and verification of our results.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) were used to assist with the writing and polishing of the manuscript. Specifically, we used LLMs to refine language, improve readability, enhance clarity, and support sentence rephrasing, grammar checking, and the overall flow of the text. LLMs were also used for literature retrieval and discovery to help identify relevant prior work and reduce the risk of overlooking closely related studies. In addition, LLMs were used to support research ideation, primarily to refine the research questions. All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the final content of the work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Model Architectures and Layerwise Representation Extraction
sections.text: This appendix provides the architectural and representation-extraction details underlying our layerwise analyses. All empirical findings are reported in the corresponding main-text and supplementary analyses.

sections.heading: Primary architecture.
sections.text: We use TabPFN-3 as the primary model for layerwise analysis ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . The pretrained model remains frozen throughout all representation and inference analyses. TabPFN-3 maps heterogeneous tabular features into fixed-dimensional row representations before performing in-context learning over rows. Its architecture consists of three stages. Stage 1 performs column-wise feature-distribution embedding through three induced-attention blocks. Stage 2 aggregates feature information within each row using three transformer blocks and four learned CLS tokens. The resulting four 128-dimensional vectors are flattened into a 512-dimensional row representation. Stage 3 applies 24 in-context-learning transformer blocks. All layerwise analyses in this paper concern these 24 Stage-3 blocks. Table 1: Architecture of TabPFN-3 used in the primary analysis. Its classification decoder is an attention-based retrieval module: support representations serve as keys, their one-hot labels as values, and query representations as queries. The decoder operates on the 512-dimensional Stage-3 representations and provides the model-native predictive readout used in our layerwise analyses.

sections.heading: A.2 Layerwise Representation Extraction
sections.text: For TabPFN-3, we extract the output representation after each of the 24 Stage-3 ICL blocks. For a query set containing n q n_{q} examples, the post-block query representation matrix at depth ℓ \ell is H q ( ℓ ) = [ h q , 1 ( ℓ ) , … , h q , n q ( ℓ ) ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ n q × 512 . H_{q}^{(\ell)}=\left[h_{q,1}^{(\ell)},\ldots,h_{q,n_{q}}^{(\ell)}\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{q}\times 512}. Each layer is represented by the row-level residual-stream output after the corresponding ICL block. The preceding feature-distribution and feature-aggregation stages are excluded from the depth index. Consequently, L0 denotes the output of the first ICL block and L23 denotes the output of the twenty-fourth and final ICL block. Support and query representations are retained at every depth. Query representations form the primary object of the representation-geometry and sample-level analyses. Support representations are used when required for class-conditioned diagnostics and model-native decoding. For the cross-model analyses, we analogously extract the post-block representation after every block in each model’s dataset-level ICL sequence. Layer indices are therefore model-specific rather than matched by absolute index across architectures.

sections.heading: Appendix B Definitions and Representation-Space Measurements
sections.text: This appendix formalizes the representation-space quantities used throughout our layerwise analyses. Unless otherwise specified, all measurements are computed independently within each dataset using the same set of query examples across layers. Cross-dataset aggregation is specified by the corresponding analysis. We characterize representation geometry through complementary quantities: PCA-based effective dimensionality describes how representation variance is distributed across principal directions; shared-PCA displacement measures sample-wise movement across depth; linear CKA and cosine similarity quantify pairwise representational similarity; and the Fisher discriminant ratio measures label-conditioned class separation.

sections.heading: B.1 Notation
sections.text: For a dataset containing n n query examples, let H ( ℓ ) = [ ( h 1 ( ℓ ) ) ⊤ ( h n ( ℓ ) ) ⊤ ] ∈ ℝ n × d H^{(\ell)}=\begin{bmatrix}(h_{1}^{(\ell)})^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ (h_{n}^{(\ell)})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} (1) denote the query representation matrix after layer ℓ \ell , where h i ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d h_{i}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the representation of query i i . For TabPFN-3, ℓ ∈ { 0 , … , 23 } \ell\in\{0,\ldots,23\} and d = 512 d=512 . We define the sample-centered representation matrix as H ~ ( ℓ ) = H ( ℓ ) − 𝟏 ​ ( h ¯ ( ℓ ) ) ⊤ , h ¯ ( ℓ ) = 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n h i ( ℓ ) . \widetilde{H}^{(\ell)}=H^{(\ell)}-\mathbf{1}\bigl(\bar{h}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{\top},\qquad\bar{h}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_{i}^{(\ell)}. (2) All layerwise comparisons use matched query examples across depth.

sections.heading: B.2 PCA-Based Effective Dimensionality
sections.text: We quantify effective dimensionality using the number of principal components required to explain a fixed fraction of the representation variance. Let σ 1 ( ℓ ) ≥ σ 2 ( ℓ ) ≥ ⋯ \sigma_{1}^{(\ell)}\geq\sigma_{2}^{(\ell)}\geq\cdots (3) denote the singular values of the centered representation matrix H ~ ( ℓ ) \widetilde{H}^{(\ell)} . The PCA-based effective dimensionality is ED ⁡ ( H ( ℓ ) ) = min ⁡ { k : ∑ j = 1 k ( σ j ( ℓ ) ) 2 ∑ j ( σ j ( ℓ ) ) 2 ≥ 0.90 } . \operatorname{ED}\!\left(H^{(\ell)}\right)=\min\left\{k:\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left(\sigma_{j}^{(\ell)}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{j}\left(\sigma_{j}^{(\ell)}\right)^{2}}\geq 0.90\right\}. (4) A larger ED indicates that representation variance is distributed across a broader set of principal directions, whereas a smaller ED indicates greater concentration of variance in fewer directions. We use the term PCA-based effective dimensionality to emphasize that this quantity is defined from the variance spectrum rather than from a nonlinear manifold estimator. The 90% retained-variance threshold is used throughout the primary analysis. Sensitivity to alternative thresholds is reported in the robustness analyses.

sections.text: To summarize the non-monotonic effective-dimensionality trajectory within each dataset, let ℓ ∗ = arg ⁡ max ℓ ​ ED ⁡ ( H ( ℓ ) ) \ell^{\ast}=\arg\max_{\ell}\operatorname{ED}\!\left(H^{(\ell)}\right) (5) denote a layer at which effective dimensionality reaches its maximum. We define the expansion ratio as ρ exp = ED ⁡ ( H ( ℓ ∗ ) ) ED ⁡ ( H ( 0 ) ) , \rho_{\mathrm{exp}}=\frac{\operatorname{ED}\!\left(H^{(\ell^{\ast})}\right)}{\operatorname{ED}\!\left(H^{(0)}\right)}, (6) and the compression ratio as ρ com = ED ⁡ ( H ( ℓ ∗ ) ) ED ⁡ ( H ( L ) ) , \rho_{\mathrm{com}}=\frac{\operatorname{ED}\!\left(H^{(\ell^{\ast})}\right)}{\operatorname{ED}\!\left(H^{(L)}\right)}, (7) where L L denotes the final analyzed layer, with L = 23 L=23 for TabPFN-3. Both quantities are computed from the complete layerwise trajectory within each dataset.

sections.heading: B.3 Representation Displacement in a Shared PCA Space
sections.text: Effective dimensionality characterizes the distribution of representation variance but does not quantify how far individual sample representations move across depth. We therefore measure adjacent-layer displacement in a shared PCA coordinate system. For each dataset, we concatenate the query representations from all analyzed layers, H joint = [ H ( 0 ) H ( 1 ) H ( L ) ] , H_{\mathrm{joint}}=\begin{bmatrix}H^{(0)}\\ H^{(1)}\\ \vdots\\ H^{(L)}\end{bmatrix}, (8) and fit PCA once to the resulting joint representation matrix. sections.text: We characterize the similarity between representations at arbitrary layers ℓ \ell and m m using two complementary measures: linear centered kernel alignment and sample-wise cosine similarity.

sections.text: To quantify label-conditioned class separation, we compute the Fisher discriminant ratio (FDR) from query representations and query labels. For class c c , let n c n_{c} denote the number of query examples belonging to that class, μ c ( ℓ ) \mu_{c}^{(\ell)} their mean representation at layer ℓ \ell , and μ ( ℓ ) \mu^{(\ell)} the global query mean. The between-class scatter matrix is S b ( ℓ ) = ∑ c n c ​ ( μ c ( ℓ ) − μ ( ℓ ) ) ​ ( μ c ( ℓ ) − μ ( ℓ ) ) ⊤ , S_{b}^{(\ell)}=\sum_{c}n_{c}\left(\mu_{c}^{(\ell)}-\mu^{(\ell)}\right)\left(\mu_{c}^{(\ell)}-\mu^{(\ell)}\right)^{\top}, (15) and the within-class scatter matrix is S w ( ℓ ) = ∑ c ∑ i : y i = c ( h i ( ℓ ) − μ c ( ℓ ) ) ( h i ( ℓ ) − μ c ( ℓ ) ) ⊤ . sections.heading: Appendix C Cross-Model Generality of Expansion–Compression
sections.text: The main analyses focus on TabPFN-3 because its 24-layer ICL stack provides a particularly clear setting in which to study depth-dependent representation dynamics. We next examine whether the broad Expansion–Compression pattern also appears in other pretrained tabular foundation models. We consider four additional models: TabPFN-v2, TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and TabICLv2. TabPFN-3 is omitted from the figures in this appendix because its representation trajectory is analyzed extensively in the main text. The purpose of the present analysis is instead to examine whether related geometric dynamics extend beyond the primary model. Across the four auxiliary architectures, the cross-dataset mean effective-dimensionality trajectories exhibit the same broad qualitative ordering: effective dimensionality increases from its initial state, reaches an intermediate maximum, and subsequently decreases. The magnitude and temporal organization of this trajectory nevertheless differ substantially across models. We therefore use Expansion–Compression to describe this recurring representation-space pattern across the models examined here, while allowing its strength and temporal organization to remain architecture dependent.

sections.heading: C.1 Cross-Model Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: For the trajectory comparison, we restrict the analysis to classification datasets for which all four auxiliary models have valid layerwise measurements. Within each dataset, the same evaluation examples are used across the compared representation measurements. Architectural details of the individual models are reported in Appendix A.1 , and all geometric quantities follow the definitions in Appendix B . Because the models differ in both representation width and initial effective dimensionality, raw ED values are not directly comparable across architectures. For visualization, we therefore normalize effective dimensionality separately within each dataset–model pair by its first-layer value, ED ^ ( ℓ ) = ED ⁡ ( H ( ℓ ) ) ED ⁡ ( H ( 0 ) ) . \widehat{\operatorname{ED}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{\operatorname{ED}(H^{(\ell)})}{\operatorname{ED}(H^{(0)})}. (18) Thus, every normalized trajectory begins at one, and values above one indicate expansion relative to that model’s own initial representation. This is not a min–max normalization. Consequently, architectures can attain different normalized peak values when their representations undergo different relative amounts of expansion. The expansion and compression ratios reported below are computed from the unnormalized within-dataset ED trajectories using the definitions in Appendix B.2 . For each dataset–model pair, the ratios are computed from its complete layerwise trajectory and are then averaged acros datasets. Because the layer attaining maximum ED can differ across datasets, the mean expansion ratio need not equal the maximum of the cross-dataset mean normalized trajectory. Final normalized ED is likewise computed within each dataset–model pair before cross-dataset averaging. Expansion, compression, and final normalized ED are therefore averaged as separate dataset-level quantities and need not satisfy an exact algebraic relation after aggregation. For PCA displacement, each adjacent-layer displacement is divided by the total displacement of the corresponding dataset–model trajectory. This allows the temporal concentration of representation movement to be compared across architectures with different overall displacement scales. The curves in Figure 10 show the original layerwise measurements together with a shape-preserving interpolation of their cross-dataset means for visualization. The interpolation affects only the rendering of the curves; all quantitative statistics are computed from the original discrete layer values.

sections.heading: C.3 Pairwise Representation Similarity
sections.text: The preceding analysis characterizes how individual geometric statistics change with depth. We additionally examine the complete pairwise relationship between representations from different layers. Figure 11 combines two complementary similarity measures. The upper triangular portion of each matrix reports linear CKA, which measures similarity in global relational structure, whereas the lower triangular portion reports mean cosine similarity, which measures directional alignment of corresponding representation vectors. Figure 11: Pairwise representation similarity across architectures. For each model, the upper triangular matrix reports mean linear CKA between every pair of layers, while the lower triangular matrix reports mean cosine similarity. Darker entries indicate greater similarity. The similarity matrices reveal substantial architecture-dependent structure that is not visible from ED alone. TabPFN-v2 and TabPFN-2.5 exhibit pronounced block-like regions in which nearby groups of layers remain highly similar, separated by transitions with lower cross-block similarity. This pattern is especially visible in the CKA matrices. TabICL and TabICLv2 show broader regions of high CKA similarity across depth. At the same time, their cosine similarity decreases more strongly between temporally distant layers. Thus, two layers can preserve a relatively similar global relational structure while their individual representation vectors undergo substantial directional reorientation. The distinction between CKA and cosine similarity is therefore informative for interpreting representation change. High CKA can coexist with substantial directional reorientation of individual vectors, while reduced cosine similarity can occur without a comparable loss of global relational structure. The two measurements provide complementary views of the same depth-dependent trajectory.

sections.heading: C.4 Scope of the Cross-Model Evidence
sections.text: Taken together, the cross-model results show that the Expansion–Compression pattern observed in the primary TabPFN-3 analysis is not unique to that architecture. Related non-monotonic ED trajectories are also present in TabPFN-v2, TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and TabICLv2. At the same time, the models differ substantially in expansion strength, compression strength, the temporal concentration of representation movement, and the continuity of their pairwise representation structure. The broad geometric pattern is therefore shared across the examined architectures, whereas its detailed organization is model dependent. The present comparison does not isolate a single architectural determinant of these differences. Model depth, hidden dimension, attention organization, decoder design, and pretraining procedure vary jointly across the model families. Identifying which of these factors determines the precise form of the trajectory therefore remains separate from the cross-model generality established here. Accordingly, the appropriate scope of the result is: the Expansion–Compression phenomenon extends beyond TabPFN-3 within the tabular foundation models examined here, while its strength and temporal organization remain architecture dependent.

sections.heading: Appendix D Architectural and Training Controls
sections.text: To characterize the conditions under which Expansion–Compression emerges, we conduct three complementary controls. We first randomize the learned weights of TabPFN-3 while preserving its architecture. We then vary computational depth within a lightweight TabPFN-style model while holding the model family and training objective fixed. Finally, we compare the resulting geometry with that of a conventionally supervised FT-Transformer. Together, these experiments separate the roles of learned parameterization, computational depth, and training paradigm in shaping the observed representation trajectory.

sections.heading: Appendix E Methodological Validation and Robustness
sections.text: This appendix provides additional methodological validation for our layerwise analysis. We first establish why the native TabPFN-3 decoder can be used as a common readout of intermediate representations, and then separate native-decoder alignment from predictive information availability using layer-matched and decoder-independent probes. Finally, we report robustness checks for the geometric quantities underlying the Expansion–Compression analysis.

sections.heading: Why the decoder is well-defined across depth.
sections.text: All 24 ICL layers preserve the same 512-dimensional hidden representation, and the decoder applies the same learned query and key projections independently of layer index. The native decoder is therefore dimensionally well-defined at every ICL layer and provides a fixed, model-native readout across depth. This does not imply a fixed decision boundary: both query and support representations evolve with ℓ \ell , changing their relative geometry and the resulting attention weights.

sections.heading: Decoder-alignment concern.
sections.text: Dimensional compatibility does not imply that native-decoder performance measures all predictive information in an intermediate representation. Earlier layers may contain label-relevant information while remaining imperfectly aligned with the final decoder, motivating tuned or layer-specific readouts ( Belrose et al., 2023 ; Balef et al., 2026 ) . We therefore distinguish predictive decodability from native-decoder alignment .

This procedure removes the requirement that an intermediate representation be aligned with the native decoder while preserving the amount of predictive information available at that layer. We evaluate both the native decoder and the layer-matched readout on all OpenML-CC18 classification tasks. sections.heading: Appendix F Candidate Competition, Early Readability, and Late Resolution
sections.text: This appendix provides the full diagnostic analyses supporting Section 4.3 . We first define the multiclass task pool and the prototype-based candidate measures used throughout the analysis, then report supplementary trajectories of candidate competition across depth, examine when class-relevant information becomes linearly readable from the attention-aggregated value stream, and finally quantify the coupling between late dimensional compression and candidate resolution.

sections.heading: F.1 Task Pool and Candidate Diagnostics
sections.text: The analysis covers all 105 multiclass classification tasks used in the main-text candidate study, including 25 tasks from OpenML-CC18 and 80 tasks from TALENT. All tasks are evaluated with the same frozen TabPFN-3 model and the same layerwise representation-extraction protocol. All diagnostic quantities are first computed at the query level, then averaged within each dataset, and finally aggregated across datasets with equal dataset weight, so that datasets with more query examples do not dominate the pooled statistics. For the difficulty-stratified analysis in Figure 4 (b), tasks are grouped according to final full-model classification accuracy. Tasks with final accuracy at least 90 % 90\% are labeled Low difficulty , tasks with final accuracy between 70 % 70\% and 90 % 90\% are labeled Medium difficulty , and tasks below 70 % 70\% are labeled High difficulty . For each layer ℓ \ell and support class c c , we construct a layer-specific prototype by averaging the support representations belonging to that class: μ c ( ℓ ) = 1 | 𝒮 c | ​ ∑ n ∈ 𝒮 c h n , s ( ℓ ) , \mu_{c}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{c}|}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{S}_{c}}h_{n,\mathrm{s}}^{(\ell)}, (28) where 𝒮 c \mathcal{S}_{c} denotes the support samples of class c c . For each query i i , we compute the cosine similarity between its layer- ℓ \ell representation and every class prototype: s i , c ( ℓ ) = cos ⁡ ( h i ( ℓ ) , μ c ( ℓ ) ) . s_{i,c}^{(\ell)}=\cos\!\left(h_{i}^{(\ell)},\mu_{c}^{(\ell)}\right). (29) Our primary measure of candidate separation is the margin between the two most similar class prototypes: Δ i ( ℓ ) = s i , ( 1 ) ( ℓ ) − s i , ( 2 ) ( ℓ ) , \Delta_{i}^{(\ell)}=s_{i,(1)}^{(\ell)}-s_{i,(2)}^{(\ell)}, (30) where s i , ( 1 ) ( ℓ ) ≥ s i , ( 2 ) ( ℓ ) s_{i,(1)}^{(\ell)}\geq s_{i,(2)}^{(\ell)} are the largest and second-largest prototype similarities. A small margin indicates that the two leading class-aligned candidates remain closely matched, whereas a large margin indicates more decisive separation. We additionally record the rank of the correct-class prototype and the correct-class top-rank rate , defined as the fraction of queries for which the correct prototype occupies rank one. To characterize the broader similarity structure across all class-aligned candidates, we also retain two supplementary diagnostics. First, we convert the prototype similarities into a normalized candidate distribution π i , c ( ℓ ) = exp ⁡ ( s i , c ( ℓ ) ) ∑ c ′ exp ⁡ ( s i , c ′ ( ℓ ) ) , \pi_{i,c}^{(\ell)}=\frac{\exp(s_{i,c}^{(\ell)})}{\sum_{c^{\prime}}\exp(s_{i,c^{\prime}}^{(\ell)})}, (31) and define the normalized candidate entropy ℋ ~ i ( ℓ ) = − ∑ c π i , c ( ℓ ) ​ log ⁡ π i , c ( ℓ ) log ⁡ C i , \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{i}^{(\ell)}=-\frac{\sum_{c}\pi_{i,c}^{(\ell)}\log\pi_{i,c}^{(\ell)}}{\log C_{i}}, (32) where C i C_{i} is the number of classes in the corresponding task. Second, we define the active candidate fraction A i ( ℓ ) = 1 C i ∑ c [ s i , c ( ℓ ) > 0.6 max c ′ s i , c ′ ( ℓ ) ] . A_{i}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{C_{i}}\sum_{c}\mathbf{1}\!\left[s_{i,c}^{(\ell)}>0.6\max_{c^{\prime}}s_{i,c^{\prime}}^{(\ell)}\right]. (33) This quantity measures the fraction of class prototypes that remain competitive under a fixed relative-similarity threshold. These two quantities serve as supplementary consistency checks rather than the primary basis of the candidate-resolution conclusion.

sections.heading: F.3 Early Readability of the Attention-Aggregated Value Stream
sections.text: We next examine whether persistent candidate ambiguity reflects the absence of class-relevant information at shallow depth. To do so, we probe the attention-aggregated value representation at every layer. For each layer, we train a linear probe on the value representation produced by learned attention-weighted aggregation, denoted attn@V . As a matched baseline, we apply the same readout to value representations aggregated with uniform attention weights, denoted uniform@V . This analysis asks when class-relevant information becomes linearly readable, rather than whether the probe reproduces the model’s native decision rule. Figure 15 (a) shows that linear readability emerges at shallow depth. Mean attn@V accuracy increases from 0.460 0.460 at L0 to 0.718 0.718 at L2, then gradually decreases to 0.600 0.600 at L23. The mean uniform@V baseline remains near 0.334 0.334 throughout. Class information is therefore highly linearly readable in the value stream well before candidate geometry reaches its strongest separation. This early-readability pattern is also prevalent at the dataset level. Figure 15 (b) compares attn@V accuracy at L2 and L23 for each of the 105 tasks. In 101 of 105 datasets, attn@V accuracy is higher at L2 than at L23. Figure 15 (c) shows the same pattern after regime-wise aggregation. Mean readability is 0.667 0.667 in the expansion regime, 0.664 0.664 in the plateau regime, and 0.607 0.607 in the compression regime. Accordingly, 101 of 105 tasks satisfy Plateau > > Compression, whereas no systematic ordering exists between Expansion and Plateau. These results separate information availability from candidate resolution : class-relevant information becomes linearly readable early, while candidate geometry continues to reorganize and reaches its strongest separation substantially later.
