Understanding Layerwise Inference in Tabular Foundation Models Wenwen Gong 1 , Haotian Gu 1 , Zhen Yang 2 , Jiaying Ma 1 , Hanqing Zhang 1 Zhongshen Wang 1 , Jingjun Wang 1 , Shouyi Xu 1 , Wei Wang 3 1 China Agricultural University 2 Tsinghua University 3 Nankai University Abstract Transformer-based tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on small to medium-sized tabular prediction tasks while processing diverse inputs through a shared stack of layers. Recent layerwise analyses identify strong predictive performance in early TFM representations and substantial overlap in computation across layers. However, early predictive accessibility alone does not establish whether later layers are dispensable for every input, and aggregate accuracy can obscure which inputs benefit from additional computation. We study all 24 in-context-learning layers of TabPFN-3 across 272 classification datasets, combining representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions, while also examining related representation dynamics in four additional TFMs. We uncover a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory, with stronger late dimensional contraction associated with larger increases in class-prototype separation. A targeted analysis of early-stabilizing samples shows that substantial representational changes persist after predicted classes stabilize, while locally ambiguous queries obtain larger accuracy gains from shallow to late layers than well-separated queries. Repeating a single pretrained block or perturbing layer order reduces predictive performance on average, constraining simple post-hoc substitutions in the frozen model. These findings distinguish predictive accessibility, class stability, and the benefits of continuing computation, supporting an input-dependent assessment of depthwise redundancy in TFMs. 1 Introduction Tabular foundation models (TFMs) ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ; Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Garg et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Ma et al., 2025 ) use in-context learning to predict on new datasets from labeled support examples, without task-specific parameter updates. A single pretrained model processes tasks with different feature spaces and class structures through the same stack of in-context-learning layers. Understanding how much different inputs benefit from this depth is important for assessing computational redundancy and identifying opportunities to reduce inference cost while preserving prediction quality ( Elbayad et al., 2020 ; Fan et al., 2020 ) . Recent layerwise analyses identify strong predictive performance in early TFM representations and substantial overlap in computation across layers ( Balef et al., 2026 ) . TabSwift ( Liu and Ye, 2026 ) further demonstrates per-query early exiting and observes that deeper exits concentrate in ambiguous regions of representation space. These findings motivate examining what subsequent computation still contributes. Early predictive accessibility does not establish that later layers are dispensable for every input, and aggregate accuracy can obscure which inputs benefit from them. Our layerwise evaluation of TabPFN-3 makes this distinction concrete. When queries are grouped by local class separation within each dataset, locally ambiguous groups show larger absolute accuracy gains from L9 to L23 on average than well-separated groups (Figure 1 (a)). Meanwhile, a targeted analysis of early-stabilizing samples shows that their representations continue to change substantially after their predicted classes stabilize, including pronounced late dimensional contraction (Figure 1 (b)). These observations highlight the need to distinguish predictive accessibility, class stability, and the accuracy gains from additional computation. They motivate our central question: When does later computation remain predictively useful, and how does its value vary across inputs? Figure 1: Predictive accessibility, class stability, and the value of depth are distinct. (a) L9/L13/L23 accuracy vs. local class separation: ambiguous queries gain more from depth. (b) Effective dimensionality per layer for early-stabilizing queries: representations keep changing after the class stabilises, then contract sharply. We study all 24 ICL layers of TabPFN-3 using 272 classification datasets from OpenML-CC18 ( Bischl et al., 2019 ) and TALENT ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . We complement its native attention-based retrieval decoder ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) with layer-matched classifiers and decoder-independent probes, combining representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions. We also examine related representation dynamics in four additional TFMs ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Grinsztajn et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) . We find that TabPFN-3 representations follow a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory: early expansion is followed by a relatively stable middle regime and substantial reorganization near the output. Class-relevant information is readable at shallow depth, while class-prototype separation strengthens mainly at later layers. Across datasets, stronger late dimensional contraction is associated with greater increases in prototype separation. These findings distinguish the early availability of predictive information from the subsequent evolution of representation geometry. At the task level, datasets with later prediction stabilization tend to incur larger accuracy losses under truncation. The overall depthwise accuracy gain also cannot be attributed entirely to mismatch with the final decoder: across 72 OpenML-CC18 tasks, accuracy increases from 82.2% at L2 to 85.6% at L23 when each layer is evaluated using its own fitted readout. Additional computation therefore retains predictive value beyond what is accessible through shallow representations under these readouts. Finally, interventions show that the frozen model is sensitive to changes in its learned layer composition. Replacing distinct blocks with repeated applications of a single pretrained block, or perturbing their execution order, alters representation dynamics and reduces predictive performance on average. These results constrain simple post-hoc substitutions within the pretrained computation. Our findings support evaluating depthwise redundancy through input-dependent predictive gains alongside the accompanying representation dynamics, and motivate future work on adaptive-depth TFM inference. 2 Related Work Tabular Foundation Models. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) build on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) to perform in-context learning without task-specific parameter updates ( Müller et al., 2022 ) . TabPFN-v1 performs ICL over row-level representations, whereas TabPFN-v2 moves to cell-level representations with alternating row- and feature-wise attention; TabPFN-2.5 largely retains this design while increasing depth and scaling to larger tables ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ; Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Grinsztajn et al., 2025 ) . In parallel, TabICL introduces a compression-then-ICL architecture that first constructs fixed-dimensional row representations, with TabICLv2 further extending this design through repeated feature grouping and target-aware representations ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) . LimiX expands structured-data foundation modeling through joint conditional prediction and retrieval-based ensemble inference ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , while TabPFN-3 combines feature grouping and row compression in a three-stage architecture ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . Despite this architectural progress, mechanistic understanding of TFM inference remains limited. Existing studies have examined spectral adaptivity ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , learned feature-space structure ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , intermediate-representation decodability ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ) , and layerwise predictive refinement and redundancy ( Balef et al., 2026 ) . Our work complements these studies by jointly examining representation geometry, sample-level prediction dynamics, and the functional role of depth. Layerwise Analysis of Transformer Representations. Layerwise analysis has been widely used to trace how information and computation evolve across Transformer depth. Probing and tuned readouts characterize when task-relevant information becomes accessible ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ; Hewitt and Manning, 2019 ; Tenney et al., 2019 ; Rogers et al., 2020 ; Belinkov, 2022 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ) , while representation-similarity and geometric analyses characterize how internal representations change across layers ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ; Ansuini et al., 2019 ; Skean et al., 2025 ) . Complementary intervention-based studies test whether individual layers or their ordering are functionally consequential ( Lad et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . Most directly, Balef et al. (2026) identify early predictive accessibility, iterative refinement, and substantial depthwise redundancy in TFMs. We extend this layerwise perspective beyond predictive readability to characterize how geometry and individual prediction trajectories evolve, and whether later transformations retain functional value. Views of Computation Across Depth. Depth has been interpreted as both iterative refinement and structured representation transformation. Residual networks can implement successive refinements of existing representations ( Jastrzebski et al., 2018 ) , whereas geometric studies report nontrivial depthwise changes in dimensionality and information structure ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ; Skean et al., 2025 ) . Related work on shared transformations and adaptive-depth inference further asks whether computation can be repeated, truncated, or selectively allocated across inputs ( Dehghani et al., 2019 ; Lan et al., 2020 ; Elbayad et al., 2020 ; Xin et al., 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2020 ) . These perspectives leave open whether TFM depth primarily reflects repetitive refinement or an ordered sequence of distinct, selectively useful transformations. 3 Experimental Setup and Analysis Framework 3.1 Experimental Setup Models. We use TabPFN-3 as the primary model for layerwise analysis ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . To assess cross-model generality, we additionally evaluate TabPFN-v2, TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and TabICLv2 ( Hollmann et al., 2025 ; Grinsztajn et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) . Architectural details are provided in Appendix A.1 , with cross-model results reported in Appendix C . Datasets and Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate binary and multiclass classification on 72 tasks from OpenML-CC18 ( Bischl et al., 2019 ) and 200 tasks from TALENT ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . We restrict the study to classification to maintain a common output space for analyzing layerwise prediction dynamics and representation geometry. All models use their standard preprocessing and inference pipelines. The layerwise representation-extraction protocol is detailed in Appendix A.2 . 3.2 Layerwise Analysis Framework Analysis framework. We analyze layerwise inference from three complementary perspectives: representation geometry, sample-dependent prediction dynamics, and the functional role of depth, building on prior layerwise probing, readout, and TFM analyses ( Alain and Bengio, 2017 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ; Kornblith et al., 2019 ; Balef et al., 2026 ) . For query i i , we denote its hidden representation after layer ℓ \ell by h i ( ℓ ) h_{i}^{(\ell)} and track its representation and prediction across depth. The representation-extraction protocol is detailed in Appendix A.2 . Predictive readout. TabPFN-3 differs from earlier TabPFN variants in replacing the fixed-width classification head with an attention-based retrieval decoder ( Grinsztajn et al., 2026 ) . The decoder predicts directly from the relationship between query and support representations: support representations serve as keys, their one-hot labels as values, and query representations as queries. Because all 24 ICL layers preserve the same 512-dimensional hidden size and the decoder uses layer-independent projections, we can apply the same pretrained model-native decoder at every depth to obtain a consistent predictive readout across layers. To control for possible mismatch between this decoder and intermediate representations, we complement the native readout with layer-matched readouts. Full decoder definitions and validation results are provided in Appendix E.1 . Representation and functional analyses. We characterize representation geometry using effective dimensionality ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ) , PCA displacement, linear CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) , and cosine similarity, capturing complementary aspects of dimensionality, movement, global structural similarity, and sample-wise directional alignment. We trace sample-level prediction trajectories and apply structural interventions to test when additional depth becomes functionally consequential ( Lad et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Balef et al., 2026 ) . Metric definitions are provided in Appendix B , with supplementary prediction-dynamics and functional analyses in Appendices G and H , respectively. 4 Expansion–Compression Emerges Across Depth 4.1 Representational Expansion Precedes Late Compression We first examine how representation geometry evolves across depth. We measure this evolution using PCA-based effective dimensionality (ED) ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ) . For the centered query representation matrix H ~ ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ n × d \widetilde{H}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with singular values σ 1 ≥ σ 2 ≥ ⋯ \sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\cdots , we define ED ⁡ ( H ( ℓ ) ) = min ⁡ { k : ∑ i = 1 k σ i 2 ∑ i σ i 2 ≥ 0.9 } . \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle\mathrm{ED}(H^{(\ell)})=\min\left\{k:\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}}\geq 0.9\right\}$}. ED measures the number of principal directions required to explain most of the representation variance. Full details are provided in Appendix B.2 . Figure 2: Representational expansion followed by late compression. Thin curves denote individual datasets and the thick curve denotes the dataset-level mean. Figure 2 reveals a pronounced non-monotonic trajectory. Effective dimensionality rises sharply at shallow depth, remains broadly elevated through the middle layers, and contracts near the output, with a brief local rebound preceding the final decline. We summarize these stages as expansion , plateau , and compression ; L9 and L17 serve only as descriptive anchors for subsequent analyses. This pattern reveals a characteristic geometric trajectory: early layers broaden the effective representational space, whereas substantial contraction emerges only near the output. We refer to this trajectory as Expansion–Compression . The pattern persists across retained-variance thresholds, normalization and covariance controls, and nearby regime boundaries. Random-weight initialization produces a qualitatively different depthwise profile (Appendix E.3 ; Appendix D.1 ). This late contraction occurs alongside continued representational change. We therefore next examine how strongly representations are reorganized within and across these regimes. 4.2 Late Compression Involves Concentrated Reorganization Figure 3: Representation transformation dynamics across depth. (a) Mean pairwise layer similarity, with linear CKA above the diagonal and cosine similarity below. (b) Adjacent-layer displacement measured in a shared PCA basis. (c) Dataset-level displacement across the expansion, plateau, and compression regimes. The ED trajectory characterizes how broadly representation variance is distributed across depth. To quantify the strength of transformation within each regime, we complement ED with pairwise layer similarity, measured by linear CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) and cosine similarity, together with adjacent-layer displacement in a shared PCA space. Metric details are provided in Appendix B.3 . Figure 3 (a) reveals distinct depthwise transformation dynamics. During expansion, representations progressively depart from earlier layers. The plateau forms a pronounced high-similarity block across both nearby and distant layers, indicating relative mid-depth stabilization. Near the output, this block breaks down as the final layers increasingly diverge from the plateau representations. Representation displacement exhibits the same structure (Figure 3 (b)). Layer-to-layer movement remains substantial during expansion, reaches its minimum through the plateau, and rises sharply again at late depth.The final layer transitions exhibit the largest concentration of PCA displacement, indicating intensified representational reorganization near the output. This concentration is consistent across datasets, with displacement lowest during the plateau and highest in the compression regime (Figure 3 (c)). Late compression therefore coincides with a concentrated phase of geometric reorganization near the output. Representation transformation intensifies again after the mid-depth plateau, showing that substantial internal reorganization persists into the final layers. 4.3 Early Predictive Accessibility Precedes Candidate Resolution To characterize the decision structure associated with this late reorganization, we analyze the geometry among competing class candidates. For each support class c c , we construct a layer-specific prototype μ c ( ℓ ) \mu_{c}^{(\ell)} and compute its cosine similarity with query i i , s i , c ( ℓ ) = cos ⁡ ( h i ( ℓ ) , μ c ( ℓ ) ) . s_{i,c}^{(\ell)}=\cos(h_{i}^{(\ell)},\mu_{c}^{(\ell)}). We quantify candidate competition by the margin between the two most similar class prototypes, Δ i ( ℓ ) = s i , ( 1 ) ( ℓ ) − s i , ( 2 ) ( ℓ ) , \Delta_{i}^{(\ell)}=s_{i,(1)}^{(\ell)}-s_{i,(2)}^{(\ell)}, and use the rank of the correct-class prototype to measure alignment with the target class. The analysis covers all 105 multiclass datasets from OpenML-CC18 and TALENT. Full diagnostic details are provided in Appendix F . Figure 4: Candidate separation strengthens at late depth. (a) Prototype margins remain small through the early and middle layers and widen most strongly near the output. (b) Correct-class alignment emerges earlier on easier tasks, whereas harder tasks retain candidate ambiguity deeper into the network. (c) Stronger late effective-dimensionality contraction is associated with larger increases in prototype margin. Figure 4 (a) shows that prototype margins remain small through the early and middle layers and widen most strongly near the output. Figure 4 (b) reveals a corresponding progression in correct-class alignment: easier tasks establish favorable alignment earlier, whereas harder tasks retain candidate ambiguity deeper into the network. Class-relevant information is already accessible well before strong candidate separation emerges. The attn@V probe exhibits strong linear class decodability by L2, whereas prototype margins widen primarily at later depth (Appendix F.3 ). Predictive accessibility therefore precedes strong geometric resolution among competing class candidates. We next relate late candidate resolution to the compression identified in Section 4.1 . For each dataset d d , we define relative late compression as C d = ED d ( 20 ) − ED d ( 23 ) ED d ( 20 ) , \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle C_{d}=\frac{\mathrm{ED}_{d}^{(20)}-\mathrm{ED}_{d}^{(23)}}{\mathrm{ED}_{d}^{(20)}}$}, and the corresponding increase in candidate separation as R d = Δ d ( 23 ) − Δ d ( 20 ) . R_{d}=\Delta_{d}^{(23)}-\Delta_{d}^{(20)}. Figure 4 (c) shows that datasets with stronger late compression exhibit larger increases in prototype margin. The same association persists across alternative specifications (Appendix F.4 ). Late dimensional contraction and candidate resolution therefore covary systematically across datasets. These results separate predictive accessibility from geometric resolution. Class-relevant information becomes readable at shallow depth while competing candidates remain weakly separated. Near the output, concentrated reorganization and compression coincide with stronger candidate separation and target-aligned geometry. Predictive accessibility therefore precedes geometric resolution. 5 Predictions Commit at Different Depths 5.1 Prediction Commitment Is Sample-Dependent Section 4.3 shows that predictive accessibility can precede geometric resolution. We next turn to the sample level and ask when the predicted class itself becomes stable. For sample i i , we denote its layerwise prediction trajectory as p i = ( y ^ i ( 0 ) , … , y ^ i ( 23 ) ) p_{i}=(\hat{y}_{i}^{(0)},\ldots,\hat{y}_{i}^{(23)}) and define the stabilization depth as the earliest layer after which the predicted class remains identical to the final-layer prediction: s i = min { ℓ : y ^ i ( k ) = y ^ i ( 23 ) , ∀ k ≥ ℓ } s_{i}=\min\{\ell:\hat{y}_{i}^{(k)}=\hat{y}_{i}^{(23)},\,\forall k\geq\ell\} . We use predictive commitment to denote this stabilization of class identity. The resulting stabilization depth s i s_{i} is a retrospective trajectory-level quantity. Confidence and representation geometry may continue to evolve after commitment. Figure 5: Sample-level predictive commitment across depth. (a) Cumulative fraction of samples stabilized to the final prediction across layers, shown per dataset and in aggregate. (b) Five recurring prediction-transition patterns and their pooled prevalence. (c) Pattern composition across tertiles of chance-normalized task difficulty; statistical analyses use difficulty as a continuous variable. Figure 5 (a) reveals substantial heterogeneity in predictive commitment. Many predictions stabilize at shallow depth, while others continue to change through intermediate or late layers, with pronounced variation across datasets. Predictions therefore commit at markedly different depths. Stabilization depth captures when a prediction becomes stable, while the preceding trajectory reveals how its class identity evolves before commitment. We characterize this trajectory using prediction identities at L9, L13, and L23 together with the total number of class transitions across all 24 layers, n chg , i = ∑ ℓ = 1 23 𝕀 [ y ^ i ( ℓ ) ≠ y ^ i ( ℓ − 1 ) ] n_{\mathrm{chg},i}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{23}\mathbb{I}\bigl[\hat{y}_{i}^{(\ell)}\neq\hat{y}_{i}^{(\ell-1)}\bigr] . Pattern assignment uses only the prediction trajectory and does not depend on ground-truth correctness. Full assignment rules are provided in Appendix G.1 , with sensitivity to nearby representative-layer choices reported in Appendix G.3 . Figure 5 (b) summarizes five recurring trajectory patterns. Early-Stable (ES) predictions reach the final predicted class early and remain there; Transient-Switch (TS) predictions temporarily depart from it before returning; Intermediate-Switch (IS) and Late-Switch (LS) predictions reach the final class at intermediate and late depth, respectively; and Multi-Switch (MS) predictions undergo repeated class changes. ES is dominant at 72.2%, followed by TS (15.8%), LS (5.8%), IS (5.3%), and MS (1.0%). Although early commitment is predominant, more than one quarter of samples exhibit non-early prediction dynamics. Similar pattern distributions are observed under dataset-level aggregation and nearby representative-layer choices (Appendices G.2 – G.3 ). Representation dynamics continue beyond early predictive commitment. Early-Stable samples have stabilized by L9, while their representations still exhibit the characteristic Expansion–Compression trajectory, including pronounced late reorganization (Appendix G.5 ). Predictive commitment can therefore precede substantial later representational transformation. More broadly, all samples traverse the same sequence of layers, while their predictions commit at substantially different depths. 5.2 Commitment Depth Tracks Task Difficulty and Local Ambiguity Commitment depth varies systematically with task difficulty and local ambiguity. At the task level, we define model-relative, chance-normalized difficulty as D d = 1 − a d − 1 / C d 1 − 1 / C d , \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle D_{d}=1-\frac{a_{d}-1/C_{d}}{1-1/C_{d}}$}, where a d a_{d} is final-layer accuracy and C d C_{d} is the number of classes. Harder tasks stabilize later on average, with a consistent association across alternative definitions of difficulty (Appendix G.4 ). Figure 6: Local class separation across prediction-transition patterns. Separation decreases from ES to MS, indicating local ambiguity for more dynamic trajectories. Correspondingly, Figure 5 (c) shows a systematic shift from ES toward non-ES trajectories as task difficulty increases. At the sample level, we quantify local ambiguity using class separation in the input space: r i = d ⁡ ( x i , NN diff ) d ⁡ ( x i , NN same ) , \scalebox{0.80}{$\displaystyle r_{i}=\frac{d\!\left(x_{i},\mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{diff}}\right)}{d\!\left(x_{i},\mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{same}}\right)}$}, where NN same \mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{same}} and NN diff \mathrm{NN}_{\mathrm{diff}} denote the nearest same- and different-class neighbors, respectively. Smaller r i r_{i} indicates greater local ambiguity. Median separation decreases from 1.52 1.52 for ES to 0.81 0.81 for MS (Figure 6 ). Dataset-aware comparisons further show higher separation for ES than for every non-ES pattern in approximately 95% of shared datasets (Appendix G.6 ). For cross-dataset analyses, we convert r i r_{i} to a within-dataset local-separation percentile to place datasets with different raw distance scales on a common reference. Lower percentiles correspond to more ambiguous samples, whereas higher percentiles indicate more clearly separated local neighborhoods. Commitment depth therefore varies systematically across both tasks and samples. Harder tasks commit later on average, while locally ambiguous samples exhibit more dynamic prediction trajectories. Thus, inputs traversing the same network can differ substantially in how much depth is required before their predictions stabilize. 6 The Functional Value of Depth 6.1 Additional Depth Has Selective Utility We next examine whether the heterogeneous commitment identified above is reflected in the functional value of additional computation at both the sample and task levels. Lower local-separation percentiles indicate greater ambiguity, whereas higher percentiles correspond to more clearly separated samples. Figure 7: Depth has selective utility across samples and tasks. (a) Accuracy at L9, L13, and L23 across within-dataset local-separation percentiles; locally ambiguous samples show larger gains with depth. (b) Retention of L9-correct predictions and rescue of L9 errors across local-separation percentiles; both increase with separation. (c) Mean stabilization depth is positively associated with L13 truncation loss. (d) Accuracy increases with depth under layer-matched readouts. At the sample level, Figure 7 (a) shows that depthwise benefit depends strongly on local ambiguity. Accuracy is already high at L9 for well-separated samples and changes only modestly toward L23, whereas the gap between shallow and final depth grows as local separation decreases. Locally ambiguous inputs therefore obtain larger aggregate gains from additional computation. To distinguish aggregate depthwise gains from the fate of individual shallow predictions, we separately measure retention of shallow successes and rescue of shallow errors: Retain = P ⁡ ( y ^ ( 23 ) = y ∣ y ^ ( 9 ) = y ) , Rescue = P ⁡ ( y ^ ( 23 ) = y ∣ y ^ ( 9 ) ≠ y ) . \mathrm{Retain}=P(\hat{y}^{(23)}=y\mid\hat{y}^{(9)}=y),\qquad\mathrm{Rescue}=P(\hat{y}^{(23)}=y\mid\hat{y}^{(9)}\neq y). Figure 7 (b) shows that both retention and rescue increase with local separation. Thus, ambiguous groups show larger aggregate gains overall, even though errors already present at L9 are less frequently rescued. The same trends hold with L8 or L10 as the shallow reference (Appendix H.2 ). The same selectivity appears at the task level. We define the loss from truncating inference at layer ℓ \ell as Δ ​ Acc d ( ℓ ) = Acc d ( 23 ) − Acc d ( ℓ ) . \Delta\mathrm{Acc}^{(\ell)}_{d}=\mathrm{Acc}^{(23)}_{d}-\mathrm{Acc}^{(\ell)}_{d}. Using L13 as the representative truncation point, Figure 7 (c) shows that datasets with later mean stabilization depth incur greater accuracy loss. The association remains positive for later truncation points and with balanced accuracy (Appendix H.1 ). Later-committing tasks are therefore more sensitive to truncation. The depthwise advantage also persists under depth-specific readouts. With independently trained layer-matched readouts, Figure 7 (d) shows that accuracy increases from 82.2 % 82.2\% at L2 to 85.6 % 85.6\% at L23. Greater depth therefore remains predictively beneficial when each layer is evaluated through its own matched readout. The functional value of depth is therefore selective: locally ambiguous samples obtain larger aggregate gains from additional computation, while later-committing tasks are more sensitive to truncation. Well-separated inputs, by contrast, gain comparatively little from the remaining layers. 6.2 Later Computation Is Ordered Rather Than Repetitive We next characterize the structure of this later computation through interventions on the ICL stack, comparing repeated shared transformations with the sequence of distinct learned blocks. Figure 8: Shared-weight repetition produces a distinct depthwise trajectory. (a) Shared-weight repetition weakens compression and class-discriminative growth. (b) The repeated-block trajectory remains distinct at matched computational depth. (c) The full model retains a predictive advantage under perturbation. Replacing the sequence of distinct ICL blocks with repeated applications of a shared block substantially weakens both late compression and class-discriminative growth (Figure 8 (a)). The effective-dimensional compression ratio decreases from 2.85 × 2.85\times to 1.05 × 1.05\times , while the FDR gain decreases from 2.53 2.53 to 0.84 0.84 . The repeated-block trajectory remains qualitatively distinct even after 24 applications (Figure 8 (b)), with the same pattern observed for representative blocks selected from different stages (Appendix H.3 ). These representational differences are accompanied by predictive differences. Under 20 % 20\% label noise, this advantage holds on every evaluated task (Appendix H.4 ). This computation path is shared across inputs, while their resolution requirements vary substantially. 7 Conclusion Interpretation. Our study clarifies when later computation remains predictively useful and how its value varies across inputs. Class-relevant information becomes accessible at shallow depth, while representation geometry continues to evolve through an Expansion–Compression trajectory, with predictive accessibility preceding geometric resolution. At the sample level, predictions commit at substantially different depths, varying systematically with task difficulty and local ambiguity. This heterogeneity is reflected in the functional value of depth: locally ambiguous samples obtain larger aggregate gains from additional computation, later-committing tasks are more sensitive to truncation, and depthwise predictive gains remain under layer-matched readouts. Structural interventions further show that later computation depends on an ordered sequence of distinct learned transformations rather than generic repetition. These findings show that TFMs follow a shared computation path whose functional value varies substantially across inputs, motivating an input-dependent view of depthwise redundancy. Limitations and Future Work. Our analysis focuses primarily on TabPFN-3 and classification, although complementary experiments reveal related representation dynamics in several additional TFMs. The strength and temporal organization of Expansion–Compression may vary across architectures and model scales. A practical early-exit mechanism will require reliable online signals that estimate whether additional computation is likely to alter or improve a prediction, rather than relying on the retrospective stabilization depth used in our analysis. Future work could investigate inference-time signals derived from prediction confidence, trajectory consistency, or representation geometry, and determine how reliably they identify inputs that benefit from continued computation. Extending these analyses to broader TFM architectures and regression settings is another important direction, particularly because regression will require suitable continuous notions of predictive commitment rather than discrete class-identity stabilization.
